We thank the reviewer for their detailed comments towards making this a truly useful reference for researchers in the field. We believe these revisions significantly improve the quality of the manuscript. Below we have point-by-point responses to their comments, including substantial additions to the MD simulation and SVD-based comparison portions of the manuscript.
We agree with the reviewer that cryo-EM datasets are diverse and present challenges beyond those offered by the analysis of TRPV1 alone. While covering the diversity of heterogeneity in cryo-EM datasets is outside the scope of this work, we have included an analysis of a second dataset that does not present some of the challenges of TRPV1: the P80S ribosome. These results reveal similar themes regarding the strengths and weaknesses of the various heterogeneity analysis methods that we saw for the TRPV1 analysis. A new subsection (Section 2.8) has been added to the end of the results section that includes a new supplemental figure (Supplementary Figure S10) and supplemental movie (Supplementary Movie 18).
Here are my main comments.
For 3DFlex, the author claimed to solve some cytosolic helices to below 3 A. However, there are no clear sidechain features visible on those helices in Figure 2. Some zoomed-in figures are needed to show those are real high resolution features instead of errors in local resolution measurement.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this nice suggestion that adds clarity to the 3DFlex results. Additional panels have been added to Figure 2A showing the clear sidechain features in the cytosolic domains for the sharpened volumes produced by 3DFlex. The following sentence has been added to the caption of Figure 2A:
Zoomed panels of the B-factor sharpened volumes show that clear atomistic details have been recovered by 3D Flexible Refinement.
Map quality in figure 4 is not as good as that in figures 2 and 3, and the map in figure 5 looks even worse. It is unclear whether it is just a difference in filtering, or an actual issue in software. It is recommended to filter the maps to the same (or at least similar) level so they can be compared visually.
Response: We thank the review for pointing this out, and we agree that the original versions of these figures were unclear. The maps in Figure 4C were reconstructions from a subset of particles. Hence there are higher levels of noise and dust. The maps from the cryoDRGN VAE in Figure 4A are of a quality comparable to those from 3DVA and 3DFlex. The maps from Figure 4A are the ones subsequently analyzed using AnaVox. We have now updated Figure 4 as follows: 1) volumes have been enlarged in Figure 4A so the detail and the similarity to the volumes in 4C are more obvious, and labels and captions have been updated to make this distinction clearer; 2) the caption in Figure 4A now reads “Volumes produced from the cryoDRGN VAE latent space display the most variation in the occupancy of the DkTx toxin, bound to the extracellular face of TRPV1, with relatively little conformational change in the protein itself.”; and 3) the caption for Figure 4C reads “Selection of particles surrounding the parts of the latent space around these clusters yields consensus reconstructions consistent with the visualizations of the cryoDRGN decoder network.”
The low map quality in Figure 5 is likely due to the filtering of particles during the ManifoldEM pipeline and is addressed in more detail in a later comment.
For the CryoDRGN results, it is quite strange to observe toxin fading gradually, instead of simply being present/absent. Is the fading density caused by subtle movement of toxin, or the imperfection of the software? As a compositional heterogeneity, it can also be analyzed by traditional focused classification. It would be a good way to quantitatively analyze the latent space distribution.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that heterogeneity methods currently have an imperfect treatment of compositional heterogeneity, showing volumes that fade gradually rather than simply being present or absent. Our understanding is that this is a current imperfection in heterogeneity methods – the tendency to produce maps that appear to be interpolations between two states, even if those intermediate states are not present in the data, as is the case for discrete heterogeneity. In general, it is a difficult problem to solve because the noise level in cryo-EM data makes it difficult to classify particles 100% accurately. However, we have added an additional figure to illustrate that the toxin binding is likely discrete. Supplementary Figure S11 has been added depicting the results of traditional 3D classification and text at line 535 onward in the Discussion section has been added to the manuscript:
An example of artifacts from these continuous latent spaces can be seen in the gradual fading of the toxin density in the volume series produced by explorations of the CryoDRGN and 3DVA latent spaces. This is despite the fact that binding of the toxin is likely discrete in nature as supported by the results of traditional 3D classification (Supplementary Figure S11).
We believe this entanglement of compositional and conformational heterogeneity is a critical point that users of these methods should be aware of, and we have elaborated on this more concretely in the Discussion section (mostly for the benefit of Reviewer 2, but it is also relevant here).
The results from ManifoldEM are not very convincing. Does it also produce other conformational changes that are more visible, like the movement of cytosolic helices shown in figure 2? It would be more convincing if the authors showed some large-scale movements that are clearly visible first to build credit for the tool, before showing the less visible small motion.
Response: We acknowledge that the volumes currently produced by ManifoldEM are not as convincing as those produced by the other tools in this paper. However, the 2D NLSA movies (Supplementary Movie 16) produced from the ManifoldEM pipeline gives insights into the heterogeneity of the sample. The lower quality of the volumes from ManifoldEM is likely due to the lower number of particles used during analysis because of the method’s intrinsic filtering of particles with low occupancies in parts of the orientation sphere. This is the likely source of the poor map quality alluded to in the reviewers previous comment. To emphasize the tools ability to detect large-scale motions, we have swapped the order of the side and top views in Figure 5. This emphasizes the fact that the same changes to the volumes can be seen in 3DVA and 3DFlex. We have also modified the text to make these points clearer and the paragraphs starting at line 229 now read:
Viewing the 2D NLSA eigenvectors derived by ManifoldEM reveals heterogeneous motions consistent with those found by other tools. When viewing PrDs derived from side views of TRPV1, changes to the conformations of the cytosolic domains are visible (Figure 5A). Whereas the PrDs from top and bottom views of TRPV1 allow one to see twists in the transmembrane domains (Figure 5B). These results are consistent with the conformational changes observed in 3DVA and 3DFlex. Additionally, the focus on projection directions appears to allow ManifoldEM to detect motions not visible to other methods. In top and bottom views of TRPV1, we could also detect changes to the size of the pore of the ion channel. This change to the size of the pore was not visible in the other methods.
While the motions depicted in the 2D NLSA movies appear consistent with other methods, the volumes produced in the final stages of Manifold Embedding are not high enough resolution to capture them. It is likely that the reason for the lower quality volumes produced by this tool is because during preprocessing for this method, any PrDs with fewer than 400 images are discarded. This results in the loss of roughly half of the particle stack from the analysis. By increasing the minimum threshold to 400 as opposed to 200 it was found that more noisy PrDs were excluded leading to an increase in the quality of the reconstructed volumes. However, this thresholding procedure results in the loss of roughly half of the particle stack from the analysis.
The MD simulation part sounds surprisingly simple for a membrane protein. The text refers to figure S2, which is not very informative. Are the lipids from the nanodisc considered in the simulation? How are the water molecules included in the simulation, particularly the water inside the channel?
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out, indeed the details of our MD simulation were too simplistic in the previous version of the manuscript. We have now added the relevant details to the methods section, including the construction of the lipid bilayer and inclusion of the solvent. Great care was taken to consider the lipids resolved in the original cryoEM density from the nanodisc. Lipids bound to the transmembrane subunits of TRPV1 were built by hand. A new panel A has been added to Figure 6, replacing Supplementary Figure 2, to give a clearer understanding of the molecular dynamics system we studied in this manuscript. The details added to the Methods section on line 685 are as follows:
The structure of TRPV1 in this dataset was solved in a nanodisc and four 1-Palmitoyl-2-oleoylphosphatidylcholine, palmitoyloleoylphosphatidylcholine (POPC) lipids are bound to the interior of the transmembrane domains. However, they have missing tails. For our simulations, these tails were built manually in VMD to ensure that these lipids and their polar contacts with the protein were preserved (Humphrey et al. 1996).
This protein-ligand system was inserted into a POPC lipid bilayer and solvated using the Charmm-GUI webserver with TIP3P water (Jo et al. 2008). The system was neutralized with sodium and chloride ions at a concentration of 0.15 mol/L. This molecular dynamics system included 78,962 water molecules, 239 chloride ions, 215 sodium ions and 424 POPC lipids. Before running molecular dynamics, the simulation box was roughly cubic, with a side length of 16 nm. The final system contained 382,773 atoms.

During equilibration, water molecules and sodium ions naturally migrated into the pore of the channel.
The MD simulation should provide much deeper insight into the dynamics of the system, instead of just being visually similar to the CryoEM analysis. For example, if the movement of the cytosolic helices from different subunits are truly correlated, what is the driving force that leads to the coordinated movement of helices from the opposite side, hundreds of Å apart? Since those helices are not interacting directly with each other, presumably there are residues at the transmembrane domain responsible for the coordination? Is it possible to identify them, maybe even mutate them in silico and show the correlation of cytosolic helical movement disappearing as a result?
Response: We thank the reviewer for these comments, and warmly welcomed the opportunity to look into molecular dynamics simulations more deeply. Indeed the analysis we performed showed several interesting insights into the allostery of TRPV1. We have included an analysis of the allosteric network in TRPV1 using the “Correlation of All Rotameric and Dynamical States” (CARDS) method (Singh, Bowman 2017). This method uses mutual information on dihedral angles to determine when conformational transitions are correlated. The results of this analysis are now shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary Figure S6A and described from line 261 onward:
Allostery is known to be crucial for TRP channels (Hilton et al 2019, Astore et al 2024). Hence, Correlation of All Rotameric and Dynamical States (CARDS) was used to detect which amino acids were responsible for transmitting allosteric information during the 5x2µs simulations run at 310 K (Sing et al 2017). This analysis revealed that the TRP box serves as a pathway for the communication of allosteric information between the cytosolic and transmembrane domains (Figure 6B). This is consistent with findings for other members of the TRPV family (Nadezhdin et al 2021, Burns et al 2023). The CARDS analysis revealed that the region surrounding amino acid K240, at the interface of the cytosolic domain and the C-terminal of the adjacent subunit, is particularly important, suggesting that any correlated motion between neighboring subunits may be mediated by this cluster of residues (Supplementary Figure S6A).
We have also calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients for the fluctuations of all four subunits in TRPV1. These results can be seen in a new panel of Supplementary Figure S6 B-C.
We agree with the reviewer that mutating residues identified as important to the allostery of TRPV1 would be of considerable interest as there are several mutations known to affect the allosteric properties of TRPV1. However, such studies would be beyond the scope of the present manuscript as we are primarily concerned here with cryo-EM methods. We expect that our simulations and the insights from the CARDS analysis in particular will guide future mutagenesis studies. In keeping with this suggestion, we have chosen to make our simulation systems and trajectories public so that it is easier to perform mutational analysis in future. We note that when the principal components of the MD simulations are visualized, the cytosolic domains appear to move in unison, but more careful study of the raw trajectories reveals that in fact the motions of these subunits are either independent or weakly anti-correlated (Supplementary Figure S6B-C).

Response: We agree with the reviewer, this section of the manuscript was indeed confusing. We hope the revisions below add clarity to our results. The reviewer is correct that changes to the pore size are difficult to see in the volumes produced by ManifoldEM, but these motions are clearly visible in Supplementary Movie 16 of the NLSA eigenvector. Notes have been added to Table 1 to clarify that some motions were only visible in the 2D NLSA movies and not the volumes.
Regarding the MD simulations, we observe the TRPV1 pore collapse during the early stages of the trajectory, which is not uncommon for channels with hydrophobic gates of this architecture. The following has been added starting at line 286:
One notable aspect of our simulations is that we observed the collapse of the hydrophobic lower gate near the beginning of each simulation (Supplementary Figure S5). However, this is a well-known phenomenon in MD simulations of channels with the six transmembrane helix (6TM) architecture (Mo et al. 2012, Shafrir et al. 2008, Jensen et al. 2010, Anishkin et al. 2004) and the other characteristics of the ligand-bound open state were preserved during the simulation.
For the SVD based comparison, there is a lack of a baseline to indicate the significance of the correlation. For example, what would be the correlation values if one generates many maps by grouping particles randomly, or just adding noise to the maps? Otherwise, it is impossible to know whether a correlation score of 0.06 means a significant agreement between two methods.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for this suggestion in particular, as it made us think more carefully about how to interpret and improve the PCV metric (see details below). We agree that it is important to have a baseline to compare the values of the captured variance. As suggested by the reviewers, we generated a series of volumes with increasing noise levels and calculated the captured variance with the series with no added noise (Sup. Fig. 14). We find that a value of log(PCV)=-2 is equivalent to the PCV found when comparing a volume series to itself with a signal to noise ratio between 10-1 and 10-2. Since this is the same value obtained when comparing series coming from two orthogonal bases in volume space (3DVA Mode 1 vs. 3DVA Mode 2), we define this value as an empirical baseline for determining if the correlation between two methods is better than that obtained by orthogonal methods. We acknowledge that this is an initial baseline test for the PCV metric, and that more comprehensive and robust tests, such as p-value analysis, could be suggested. We will defer these to future work.
We would like to note that while addressing this comment we found an error in the code that calculates PCV – we were not squaring Equation 3 in our code. This has now been fixed and all related figures have been updated with the correct results. Note also that these results are now reported as base 10 logarithms. This error did not change the qualitative trends of our results. Additionally, we have chosen to rebrand cryoSVD as “AnaVox” (short for Analysis of voxel maps), to communicate the broader scope of this Python package, and improved the PCV metric definition as described below.
The following has been added to the manuscript at line 366:
Interpreting summary statistics like PCV is nontrivial. For voxel maps in high dimensional spaces, it is more likely for randomly chosen unit vectors to be orthogonal rather than parallel and have a dot product close to zero. Hence, to help interpret the absolute magnitude of the PCV metric, we have designed simple experiments to learn how PCV changes in different situations. By adding white noise to a series of volumes, we can use PCV to compare how the eigenvectors change as a function of the noise level (Supplementary Figure S14A). We find that a log(PCV) of -2 would correspond to a signal to noise ratio (SNR) of between 10−1 and 10−2. This PCV score is the same as what we obtained when comparing modes 1 and 2 of 3DVA, a method that gives us orthogonal components in volume space (Figure 8C, Supplementary Figure S9), indicating that there is no significant correlation between two volume series with log(PCV)< −2. For example, in the case of 3DVA mode 1 (Supplementary Figure S14B) at a SNR of 10−1 the outline of the original eigenvector is still visible, however, by 10−2 it is no longer visible.
In addition, to make our PCV metric more informative, we have decided to compute this quantity in an asymmetric way. That is, in the previous revision we were computing PCV(A, B) = ½ d(U_A, V_B, S_B) + ½ d(V_B, U_A, S_A), and now we are have changed to simply computing PCV(A, B) = d(U_A, V_B, S_B). The reason being that this asymmetric form of PCV communicates how well the basis of one volume series spans another. Equation 3 now reflects this revision. An example of this asymmetry is given in Supplementary Figure S12 and line 822 now reads:
Notice that this metric is asymmetric, meaning that instances exist where PCV (A, B) < PCV (B, A) or vice versa. PCV (A, B) is a measure of how well A covers B, and there can be cases where A covers B well but B does not cover A well. An illustrative example of the asymmetric PCV metric is given in Supplementary Figure S12.
For SVD comparison, what has the author done to avoid the different filtering in the maps, as well as the SNR caused by particle count? Would the correlation values be different if we simply lowpass filter every map to 5 or 10Å? Would it matter if only a subset of particles were used in the reconstruction?
Response: The reviewer poses valid concerns. Filtering of maps and changes in SNR will cause changes to SVD comparisons. Supplementary Figure S14A shows the effects of adding noise to volume series, and Supplementary Figure S14C shows the effects of low pass filtering on the volumes. Although the PCV matrix values exhibit some changes, we observe that some low-pass filtering or adding some levels of noise does not produce significant effects. To clarify this we have added the text at line 379:
It is also of interest what the contributions of different frequencies are to the PCV. We found that low pass filtering of the volumes does not greatly change their relative PCVs up to a low-pass filtering of 14 A. This is consistent with the finding that linear bases of voxel maps are most sensitive to low resolution features (Supplementary Figure S14C-D) (Sorzano, Carazo et al. 2021).
The consideration of different numbers of particles is beyond the scope of cryoSVD (now AnaVox) itself as it relates to the SNRs of the volumes. We believe this will be a powerful tool for comparing series of volumes, it is agnostic to how those volumes were produced. A case study of the effects of changing particle count can be found in supplementary Figure S13 where we analysed the volume series presented from independent half-sets of the particle images. This will be described in full in a later comment.
Also for the SVD based comparison, it seems that only movement trajectories along eigen-vectors are considered? What if one method describes a movement as a straight path and the other as a curve in the latent space?
Response: We share the reviewer's interest in exploring trajectories in high dimensional latent spaces. In fact, this is precisely the reason we developed cryoSVD (now AnaVox) — to compare volume series. If one method describes a straight path through a latent space, and another trajectory is curved, AnaVox is still capable of comparing both these volume series. It is agnostic to how those voxel series were produced. Our PCV metric compares the basis spanned by the eigenvectors of these series in voxel space, not the latent space of the method that produced them. Since this paper focuses on comparing the outputs of different heterogeneity methods, it is logical to compare the volumes produced by sampling in a straight line along the eigenvectors of the latent space of the source method, as this represents their typical outputs. However, one can use this pipeline to compare any two volume series to see if they contain the same heterogeneous motion. The following has been added on line 329:
This tool can be used to compare any two volume series to determine if they contain the same molecular heterogeneity. However, here we will use it to compare volume series derived from the eigenvectors from the latent spaces of different methods.
To further validate the comparison method, maybe break the datasets to two halves and analyze the heterogeneity in each set separately. This will show whether the correlation is consistent and what is the noise level in the comparison. It still won’t overcome any potential systematic bias but should be a step forward.
Response: This was a very useful suggestion by the reviewer and we learned a lot attempting to address this point. To further validate our comparison methods, we split the dataset into two halves and ran heterogeneity analysis on each set separately. We found that without downsampling the particle stacks our results showed poor correlation, indicating a low signal to noise ratio. We reran our analysis on independent half-sets of the data with cryoDRGN and 3DVA. These results show that the volume series from the different half-sets correlate well with each other. However, we did find some notable differences in their power spectrums which appear to be from different low frequency noise between the two half-sets. Supplementary Figure S13 has been added with these results and the following paragraph has been added to line 395 of the manuscript:
To gain an understanding of how robust heterogeneity analysis is to particle count, we applied 3DVA and cryoDRGN to independent half-sets of the particle images. Each half-set contained 109,393 particles. At first we found that the results between the half-sets differed significantly. By down sampling the images and applying symmetry expansion, the results between the half-sets became more similar. With this preprocessing, we used AnaVox to demonstrate that each method delineates the same molecular motions in each half-set. The volume series for the same method in different half-sets are visually very similar and they follow similar paths when projected into a common basis (Supplementary Figure S13A). This confirms that they capture the same molecular motions in each half-set. Calculating the PCV for the volume series from different half-sets, we can see that the same method from different half-sets shares a high PCV, confirming that they capture the same molecular heterogeneity (Supplementary Figure S13B). However, the PCV scores indicate that the bases for different half-sets are not the same when comparing across different methods, indicating some differences between them. For example, the first 3DVA mode in the first half-set is more similar to the cryoDRGN results than the first 3DVA mode in the second half-set. Visual analysis of the volume series and inspection of their power series indicate that these differences are most likely due to low-frequency noise in the region surrounding the nanodisc (Supplementary Figure S13C).
The nanodisc subtraction strategy might be problematic. Typically for focused alignment, we remove the density of rigid parts by subtracting the projections of averaged structures from the particle images. In this case, we already know the nanodisc is highly variable, so the average structure does not reflect the actual nanodisc density in each particle, resulting in leftover density of different sizes and shapes. Even though it does not have a major impact on homogeneous reconstructions, they may be interpreted as structural variability, and might be the main cause of the heterogeneity at the transmembrane domain reported by CryoDRGN and ManifoldEM.
Response: We share the reviewer’s concerns about proper treatment of nanodisc heterogeneity. Signal subtraction, indeed, is not an optimal solution, as it uses a static mask to treat the heterogeneous signal of the nanodisc. Thus, in the long run we believe that more rigorous forms of signal subtraction are necessary for heterogeneous ensembles. This influenced our addition to the AnaVox results section on line 413:
This highlights the need for more robust methods to filter structured noise from a dataset during heterogeneity analysis.
To ensure that, as the reviewer is concerned, we have not biased our analysis of protein conformational heterogeneity by the process of nanodisc signal subtraction, we have now conducted both the 3DVA and cryoDRGN analyses with and without signal subtraction. We found the same heterogeneity in the transmembrane domains in the volume series produced both with and without signal subtraction. The following has been added to the first Methods Section, elaborating on the nanodisc subtraction procedure on line 596:
For completeness, we conducted 3DVA and cryoDRGN on both the signal subtracted and non-signal subtracted data. When viewing the volumes at high thresholds and carefully exploring the latent spaces of each method, we found the same heterogeneity within the transmembrane region of the protein, indicating that the signal-subtraction procedure is likely not biasing our results (Supplementary Movie 17).
Finally, the newly included heterogeneity analysis of the ribosome shows how the same qualitative trends between methods are reproduced even without signal subtraction.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This study provides a survey of tools designed to extract information on conformational heterogeneity from cryo-EM data sets, specifically evaluating five existing software packages using the data observing the TRPV1 protein complex. The authors describe similarities and differences in the output of each tool.
It is difficult to discern the main conclusions of the manuscript. While the authors discuss which aspects of heterogeneity each technique may capture more effectively, it remains unclear how these findings can guide the broader research community in analyzing other systems because this investigation focuses solely on TRPV1.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback. We believe this work is useful as a guide to the broader research community in analyzing other systems, but also hope our findings highlight the current differences in the results of existing methods for analyzing conformational heterogeneity in cryo-EM. The reviewer’s suggestions have motivated us to 1) add a supplemental analysis of a ribosome dataset and 2) clarify the goals and findings of our manuscript, emphasizing what is novel and important about our work.
1) In the additional analysis of the P80S ribosome we see similar trends to our TRPV1 analysis -- see new subsection 2.8, including a new supplemental figure (Figure S10) and supplemental movie.
2) This work represents the most comprehensive study comparing the heterogeneity of a single experimental dataset with multiple methods to date. With this one dataset we are able to address how different algorithms confound compositional and conformational heterogeneity and the complicating issue of nanodisc heterogeneity for membrane proteins. While this paper starts with qualitative comparisons of different approaches to analyze heterogeneity, we conclude by presenting various metrics for assessing heterogeneity in cryo-EM data, namely comparisons with molecular dynamics simulations through Bayesian ensemble reweighting or by using the AnaVox tool newly presented here. Overall, while we are encouraged by all the new approaches to heterogeneity in cryo-EM, we want to emphasize to readers that heterogeneity in cryo-EM remains a hard problem, and methods still need to be pushed forward by comparing and critiquing methods as possible. We have added clarifying text to this effect in the Abstract, Introduction, and Discussion & Conclusion sections:
(Introduction line 49): The increasing number of heterogeneity tools in the literature motivated us to perform the most rigorous study of heterogeneity in a biologically relevant sample to date and determine if these tools provide complementary or orthogonal information. … In this vein, we also developed a software framework called AnaVox to quantitatively determine whether two heterogeneity methods agree with each other.
(Introduction line 100): Hence, we developed the software package AnaVox to quantitatively determine whether two volume series capture the same heterogeneity signal and also characterise the presence of compositional heterogeneity.
(Discussion lines 453 onward): Overall we have found that for both the TRPV1 and the ribosome datasets we analyzed, different heterogeneity analysis methods more preferentially analyze compositional vs. conformational heterogeneity when both are present in a sample.
This study was motivated by the promise of computational tools to access heterogeneous molecular states in single particle cryo-EM data. However, our results demonstrate that while existing software tools are able to reveal the presence of this heterogeneity, they are not yet capable of enabling quantitative biophysics. This is apparent from the differing sensitivity and stochasticity of each tool. For example, the nature of the VAE architecture in cryoDRGN appears to make it especially sensitive to compositional heterogeneity. On the other hand, the volume preserving flow field of 3DFlex limits it to the detection of conformational heterogeneity. Outside these extremes, we found these tools tend to convolve the two kinds of heterogeneity. For this dataset, all of the methods we used produce clear evidence of a spectrum of states. However, the cryoDRGN result clearly indicates a population of channels in the apo closed state, but in combination with the results of the other methods, we also believe there is significant heterogeneity within the ligand bound states. Characterising the independent heterogeneous motion of the two states appears to be beyond the capability of the current generation of tools. This work establishes the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches to the study of heterogeneity. However, continued software development in this space is still needed before these tools can be used for quantitative biophysical investigations of macromolecules by cryo-EM practitioners.
(Discussion lines 556 onward): Overall, this study of molecular heterogeneity in a real dataset serves as a proof of concept for more ambitious experiments that can exploit the heterogeneity of vitrified samples in cryo-EM. With the analysis of these datasets we have demonstrated the AnaVox pipeline as well as discussed issues with the entanglement of compositional and conformational heterogeneity, which we believe is a key issue for methods developers to tackle in the future. We have even suggested an initial solution in this direction, by presenting the mean power spectrum variance for each method.
In this regard, the cited paper 31 [CryoBench], co-authored by some of the present authors, appears to address a similar goal but on a wider scale.
Response: Although the motivations of CryoBench and this work are similar, there is a key difference in that the datasets analyzed in this work are experimentally collected datasets. CryoBench presents synthetic datasets as benchmarks for heterogeneity analysis in cryo-EM, while here we address the performance of a variety of heterogeneity methods on real datasets, with all the complications, nuances, and uncontrolled variables that implies, where no ground truth is available. In this work we consider practical considerations relevant to these analyses that cannot be captured from the analysis of synthetic data. Both the approach of CryoBench and the approach presented here are necessary and meaningful. To clarify this point, the following has been added to the Introduction on line 52:
While a similar task has been performed using ground truth volumes with synthetic data (Jeon et al 2024), the study presented here provides comparison metrics and validation tools when using real data for which no ground truth is available.
On the other hand, if the primary goal of the study is to provide a comprehensive overview of the software, the descriptions of the methods and procedures seem too brief to be of practical use to the reader.
Response: Indeed the primary goal of this study is not to provide a comprehensive overview of the software, but to rather be a guide to the reader of our experiences of using these tools to tackle one experimental cryo-EM dataset with different methods and how we have gone about comparing the results. We hope that the additions to the reviewer’s first comment help to clarify this. We refer the reader to the original papers and documentation for the practical application of each method. We have also expanded the Methods sections where we have gone above and beyond the standard use of each method to help inform the readers on how we have found the specific results from the tools presented in this study.
